title: INT 16h, the keyboard services
covers: INT 16h, the keyboard services: reading, checking and storing keystrokes, shift states, the DOS/V and PC country calls, and the AX PC, ETen, J-3100 and Word cooperation calls.

rows.text: INT 16h AH=00h gets a keystroke.
AH is the BIOS scan code.
AL is the ASCII character.
On extended keyboards this function discards extended keystrokes and returns only when a non-extended keystroke is available.
The BIOS scan code is usually, but not always, the hardware scan code: it differs for shifted special keys.
Some older clone BIOSes do not discard extended keystrokes and manage AH=00h and AH=10h the same.
The K3PLUS v6.00+ INT 16 BIOS replacement does not discard extended keystrokes but translates prefix E0h to 00h.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x00 of its dispatch on AH.
On PC-98 with the break flag set the case stores AX 0 and returns without reading the buffer.
When the configuration asks for it the case unmasks IRQ1 on every read.
With no non-extended key available it adds one to reg_ip and returns, so the callback runs again.
The case also stores INT28_AllowOnce true.
INT 16h AH=10h gets an enhanced keystroke, on enhanced keyboards only.
AH is the BIOS scan code.
AL is the ASCII character.
If no keystroke is available, the function waits until one is placed in the keyboard buffer.
The BIOS scan code is usually, but not always, the hardware scan code, and differs for shifted special keys.
Unlike AH=00h, this function does not discard extended keystrokes.
INT 16/AH=09h tells whether the function is supported, but only on later model PS/2s.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x10 of its dispatch on AH.
On PC-98 with the break flag set the case stores AX 0 and returns without reading the buffer.
With no key available it adds one to reg_ip and returns, so the callback runs again.
For an enhanced key whose low byte is F0h the case clears the low byte unless the key is a Kanji code.
When configured the case unmasks IRQ1, and it also stores INT28_AllowOnce true.
INT 16h AH=01h checks for a keystroke.
ZF is set if no keystroke is available.
ZF is clear if a keystroke is available.
With a keystroke available, AH is the BIOS scan code.
With a keystroke available, AL is the ASCII character.
A keystroke present is not removed from the buffer, but extended keystrokes incompatible with 83/84-key keyboards are removed by IBM and most compatible BIOSes.
Some older clone BIOSes do not discard extended keystrokes and manage AH=00h and AH=10h the same.
The K3PLUS v6.00+ replacement does not discard extended keystrokes but translates prefix E0h to 00h.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x01 of its dispatch on AH.
With int16_ah_01_cf_undoc set the case also sets CF when a key is available and clears it otherwise.
The case enables interrupts after IRET, unmasks IRQ1 when configured, and stores INT28_AllowOnce true.
INT 16h AH=11h checks for an enhanced keystroke, on enhanced keyboards only.
ZF is set if no keystroke is available.
ZF is clear if a keystroke is available.
With a keystroke available, AH is the BIOS scan code.
With a keystroke available, AL is the ASCII character.
A keystroke available is not removed from the buffer, and unlike AH=01h extended keystrokes are not discarded.
Some versions of the IBM BIOS Technical Reference erroneously report CF instead of ZF.
INT 16/AH=09h tells whether the function is supported, but only on later model PS/2s.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x11 of its dispatch on AH.
For an enhanced key whose low byte is F0h the case clears the low byte before returning it.
The case enables interrupts after IRET, unmasks IRQ1 when configured, and stores INT28_AllowOnce true.
INT 16h AH=02h gets the shift flags.
AL is the shift flags (see #00582).
AH is destroyed by many BIOSes.
Shift flags: bit 7 Insert, bit 6 CapsLock, bit 5 NumLock, bit 4 ScrollLock, bit 3 Alt pressed, bit 2 Ctrl pressed, bit 1 left shift, bit 0 right shift.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x02 of its dispatch on AH.
The case leaves AH unchanged.
INT 16h AH=03h sets the typematic rate and delay.
AL is the subfunction: 00h sets default values, 01h to 04h change PCjr values, 05h sets the rate and delay, 06h gets them.
With AL=05h, BH is the delay value, 00h 250ms to 03h 1000ms.
With AL=05h, BL is the repeat rate, 00h 30 per second to 1Fh 2 per second.
With AL=06h, BL returns the repeat rate.
With AL=06h, BH returns the delay.
AH is destroyed by many BIOSes.
INT 16/AH=09h tells whether some of the subfunctions are supported.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x03 of its dispatch on AH.
The case handles only AL 0x00 and 0x05 and logs an error for every other value, PCjr subfunctions included.
The case answers AL=06h with a logged error and stores no rate or delay.
The case answers AL=06h with a logged error and stores no rate or delay.
The case never stores AH and leaves it as the caller left it.
AL=00h writes F3h then 20h, the 500ms delay and 30 characters per second defaults.
INT 16h AH=05h stores a keystroke in the keyboard buffer, on AT and PS machines with enhanced keyboards.
CH is the BIOS scan code.
CL is the ASCII character.
AL is the status: 00h if successful, 01h if the keyboard buffer is full.
AH is destroyed by many BIOSes.
Under DESQview and on the HP 100LX and 200LX, some keystrokes invoke special functions when read from the buffer (see #00583 and #00584).
DESQview pseudo-keystroke 38FBh switches to the next window only if the main menu is already popped up, and 38FCh pops up the main menu.
HP 100LX/200LX pseudo-keystroke EE00h pops up the topcard display and puts other system manager applications into sleep mode.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x05 of its dispatch on AH.
The case never stores AH and leaves it as the caller left it.
DESQview pseudo-keystroke 38FEh closes the current window, and 38FFh pops up the learn menu.
INT 16h AH=12h gets the extended shift states, on enhanced keyboards only.
AL is shift flags 1, the same as AH=02h returns (see #00587).
AH is shift flags 2 (see #00588).
AL bit 3 is set only for the left Alt key on many machines, and AH bits 7 through 4 are always clear on a Compaq SLT/286.
INT 16/AH=09h tells whether the function is supported, but only on later model PS/2s.
Many BIOSes destroy AH on return from functions above AH=12h, returning 12h less than AH held on entry.
Shift flags 1: Insert, CapsLock, NumLock, ScrollLock, Alt, Ctrl, left shift and right shift in bits 7 to 0.
Shift flags 2: SysReq, CapsLock pressed, NumLock pressed, ScrollLock pressed, right Alt, right Ctrl, left Alt and left Ctrl in bits 7 to 0.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x12 of its dispatch on AH.
The case builds AH from the BIOS flag bytes: bits 0-1 and 4-6 of FLAGS2, its bit 2 moved to bit 7, and bits 2-3 of FLAGS3.
INT 16h AH=13h is the DOS/V double-byte character set shift control.
AL is the function: 00h sets the shift status from DX.
The functions are supplied by the Japanese Front-End Processor.
Shift status: bit 0 full-size rather than half-size, bits 2-1 the input mode, bits 5-3 internal, bit 6 Romaji, bit 7 Katakana to Kanji conversion, bits 15-8 internal.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x13 of its dispatch on AH.
The case sets or reads the host input method state and stores DL 0x81 or 0x00, not a shift status built from the Japanese Front-End Processor.
For AL=00h the case switches the host input method on or off from bit 7 or 0 of DL and stores no shift status.
The case acts only when (IS_DOSV or ttf_dosv) and IS_DOS_CJK hold and DOSV_FEP_CTRL_IAS is set; otherwise it changes nothing.
With AL=01h, DX returns the current shift status (see #00589).

rows.text: INT 16h AH=14h controls the shift status display.
AL is the function: 00h enables the display, 01h disables it, 02h gets the display state.
With AL=02h, AL returns the current state, 00h enabled or 01h disabled.
It controls the screen-bottom shift status rows for the Japanese Front-End Processor.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x14 of its dispatch on AH.
The case acts only when (IS_DOSV or ttf_dosv) and IS_DOS_CJK hold and DOSV_FEP_CTRL_IAS is set; otherwise it changes nothing.

rows.text: INT 16h AH=50h sets or gets the keyboard BIOS country mode by AL.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x50 of its dispatch on AH.
On a machine that is not a JEGA the case returns at once, changing nothing.
An AL no case takes logs an error and stores AL 0x02.
INT 16h AX=5000h sets the keyboard country code, on AX PC machines.
BX is the country code, 0001h USA (English) or 0051h Japan.
AL is the status: 00h successful, 01h bad country code, 02h other error.
Japanese versions of MS-DOS, PC DOS and DR DOS call it with BX=0051h at initialization.
The K3PLUS v6.00+ replacement switches country layouts, or to transparent mode, and beeps on mode changes.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x50, then by case 0x00 of the dispatch on AL.
On a machine that is not a JEGA the case returns at once, changing nothing.
INT 16h AX=5001h gets the keyboard country code, on AX PC machines.
AL is the status: 00h successful with BX holding the country code, 02h error.
The call is also supported by K3PLUS v6.00+.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by the case 0x50, then by case 0x01 of the dispatch on AL.
On a machine that is not a JEGA the case returns at once, changing nothing.
On an AX PC, AH=51h reads the shift key status.
AL is the standard shift key states.
AH is the Kana lock: 00h when off, 01h when on.
The K3PLUS v6.00+ INT 16 replacement also supports the call, but always returns AH=00h.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by case 0x51 of its dispatch on AH.
Outside a JEGA machine, or outside its JP keyboard mode, the case returns with every register unchanged.
AH receives the status byte masked with 0x02, so the Kana lock reads 0x02, not the document's 01h.
AX=5500h is Microsoft Word's internal cooperation call, made at startup to any keyboard TSR present.
AX is 4D53h ('MS') if a keyboard TSR is present.
If the return is not 4D53h, Word installs its own INT 09 and INT 16 handlers; otherwise it assumes the TSR handles the keyboard.
AX=55FEh is Microsoft QBASIC's internal cooperation call: DX=0000h initializes with a function and structure pointer, DX=FFFFh shuts down.
AX is the result: 4D4Bh installs only the INT 1B handler, and any other value also installs handlers for INT 08, 09, 16, 1B and 1C.
The pointer in ES:CX seems to point at a structure defining a keyboard callback; a TSR returning AX=4D4Bh makes QBASIC stop.
MS-DOS 6.0's DOSSHELL makes these calls at startup, exit and before or after shelling out; EDIT.COM and HELP.COM do too, through QBASIC.
K3PLUS v6.07+ supports this function but never invokes the callback function.
AX=55FFh is a Microsoft Word call whose TSR cooperation is unknown; BX holds Word's version, BL its major part.
CX=0000h sets an unknown flag and any other value clears it.
Hooks intercepting this call are present in SWAPSH, SWAPDT v1.77j and SCRNBLNK.COM, and the German Word 5.0 calls it.
The INT 16h handler reaches it by case 0x55 of its dispatch on AH.
AX is left at 0x55FEh, which the document reads as the other result that installs handlers, and no handler is installed.
The case stores nothing: AX is left unchanged, never 4D53h; it only logs at src/ints/bios_keyboard.cpp:1529.

rows.text: The INT 16h handler reaches it by case 0xF5 of its dispatch on AH.
The key is stored only where J3_IsJapanese() holds, on a J-3100 in video mode 74h; elsewhere every register is left unchanged.
BX holds the key, which is handed to BIOS_AddKeyToBuffer.
AX becomes 0000h when the key is stored and FFFFh when the buffer is full.

rows.text: The INT 16h handler reaches it by case 0xF6 of its dispatch on AH.
The buffer is counted only where J3_IsJapanese() holds, on a J-3100 in video mode 74h; elsewhere every register is left unchanged.
AX counts the keys between tail and head, halved, and becomes FFFFh when that equals the buffer size in words.
BX becomes the machine code of the emulated J-3100 model.
On PC-98 the store, read and check helpers of the same file take head and tail from 0x524 and 0x526.
